newsitem.title: FRANCE: Alarmed world pleads for Middle East crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Alarmed world pleads for Middle East crisis talks.

text.p: An alarmed world pleaded with Israeli and Palestinian leaders on Friday to meet and try to halt bloodshed triggered by Israeli archaeological excavations in Jerusalem's Old City, and some officials voiced fears of war.

The leaders of France, Britain and Germany made an unprecedented joint appeal to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to meet immediately to calm violence raging in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

In almost identical letters to the two leaders, President Jacques Chirac, Prime Minister John Major and Chancellor Helmut Kohl said: "We are sending you a joint, solemn appeal to make the necessary calming gestures."

The United States told Israel and the Palestinians that the violence must stop. President Bill Clinton, avoiding outright condemnation of Israel, appealed to both sides to stop the violence and "avoid unnecessarily provocative actions".

Diplomatic sources said Netanyahu rebuffed a request from U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher to seal off a disputed ancient tunnel near Al-Aqsa Mosque, one of Islam's holiest shrines, which triggered the worst fighting since the 1993 Israel-PLO peace accords.

In New York, Christopher planned to meet Israeli, Egyptian and Syrian foreign ministers as the United States kept up furious telephone diplomacy to try to end the fighting which has killed 53 Palestinians and 14 Israeli soldiers.
Russia accused Israel of stalling the Middle East peace process and urged both sides to back away from confrontation.
Intensive diplomacy involving several powers was under way to persuade Netanyahu and Arafat to meet, possibly in Cairo, but each was setting conditions unacceptable to the other, diplomats said.
Despite American reluctance, the U.N. Security Council met in New York to discuss the violence amid fears that Washington's five-year-old regional peace policy could collapse.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy told the meeting his country would not accept the blame for the crisis and called on Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to impose order.

Western politicians and media overwhelmingly blamed Netanyahu for provoking a new Palestinian uprising, not just by ordering the opening of the tunnel, but by dragging his feet in peace talks and refusing to carry out a withdrawal from Hebron agreed by his predecessors.
Austrian Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel said the Middle East was entering "a really dramatic situation" and expressed concern the violence could get out of control.
Schuessel said the Middle East peace process had taken a step back during Netanyahu's first 100 days in office and urged Palestinians and Israelis to return to the table.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, in New York to for the U.N. General Assembly, told the BBC: "The peace process has to be revived and it has to be revived in a substantive way.

"The Israeli government have said they are prepared to continue with the commitment of their predecessors to withdraw from Hebron. I think this would be a symbolic movement to actually give that a kick start, to get that moving again, and to demonstrate that Mr Netenyahu's government is commited to the peace process even if they do differ in certain important respects from their predecessors...," he added.

The Washington Post newpaper commented: "No one even slightly familar with the immense volatility of the Jerusalem issue could have imagined that Israel would on its own make a significant change on the ground, on the edge of a site sacred to Moslems as well as Jews, without triggering an enraged Palestinian response."
The Netanyahu government's go-slow approach to peace talks had already severely eroded Palestinian patience, making a popular eruption "almost inevitable", the U.S. newspaper added.

Former German foreign minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher, a veteran friend of the Jewish state, said past Labour governments had turned over a "precious inheritance" to Netanyahu -- "the chance for lasting peace between Palestinians and Israelis".

The pro-Israeli daily Die Welt questioned whether Arafat could stop the violent reaction of his people and raised the possibility of a slaughter of Jewish settlers isolated in the occupied territories.
No one outside Israel backed Netanyahu's assertion that the violence was deliberately planned by Arafat's self-rule Palestinian Authority.

French commentators said the dangerous difference between the stone-throwing 1987-93 Palestinian Intifada, or uprising, and the latest explosion was that the Palestinians now had 30,000 armed police facing the might of the Israeli army.
The Irish Times, in a commentary typical of many Western newspapers, said Netanyahu was guilty of either deliberate provocation or "arrogant incompetence".

Igor Mann, one of Italy's most respected commentators on the Middle East, wrote in La Stampa newspaper: "Benjamin Nethanyahu has conducted an insensitive, irresponsible policy. He promised the Israeli people 'peace and security' and this is the result."
